# The Huygens–Steiner (Parallel Axis) Theorem

**Claim.** Let $B$ be a body of mass $M$, let $I_0$ be its moment of inertia about an axis $A$ through its centre of mass, and let $I$ be its moment of inertia about an axis $A'$ parallel to $A$, at distance $l$ from $A$. Then
$$I \;=\; I_0 + M l^2 .$$

The claim is **true**. We prove it below, after making all the notions involved precise. The proof covers simultaneously the case of a finite system of point masses, of mass distributed with a density over a curve, a surface or a solid, and of any mixture of these, since all of these are instances of a mass measure.

---

## 1. Definitions and standing hypotheses

We work in Euclidean $3$-space $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the standard inner product $u \cdot v$ and norm $|u| = \sqrt{u\cdot u}$.

**Definition 1 (Body / mass distribution).**
A *body* $B$ is modelled by its *mass distribution*: a Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, where for a Borel set $E$ the number $\mu(E)$ is the mass of the part of $B$ occupying $E$. Its *mass* is
$$M := \mu(\mathbb{R}^3),$$
and we assume throughout that
$$0 < M < \infty. \tag{H1}$$
We write $dm$ for $d\mu(r)$ inside integrals, as is customary in mechanics.

*Examples.* (i) A system of point masses $m_1,\dots,m_N$ at positions $r_1,\dots,r_N$ corresponds to $\mu=\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\,\delta_{r_i}$, for which $\int f\,dm=\sum_i m_i f(r_i)$. (ii) A solid occupying a region $V$ with density $\rho$ corresponds to $d\mu=\rho\,\mathbf{1}_V\,dV$, for which $\int f\,dm=\int_V f\rho\,dV$. (iii) A lamina or a wire corresponds to a density against $2$- or $1$-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Everything below applies verbatim to each of these.

**Definition 2 (Axis; parallel axes).**
An *axis* is a straight line in $\mathbb{R}^3$, i.e. a set of the form
$$L=L(p,n)=\{\,p+tn \;:\; t\in\mathbb{R}\,\},\qquad p\in\mathbb{R}^3,\ n\in\mathbb{R}^3,\ |n|=1 .$$
Two axes are *parallel* if they have the same direction, i.e. if they can be written as $L(p,n)$ and $L(p',n)$ with one and the same unit vector $n$. (Replacing $n$ by $-n$ describes the same line, so "having the same direction" is a property of the pair of lines, not of the chosen parametrisations. Two such lines are automatically coplanar: if $n$ and $p'-p$ are linearly independent they both lie in the plane through $p$ spanned by $n$ and $p'-p$, and otherwise they coincide. So this agrees with the classical definition of parallel lines, except that the classical definition also requires the two lines to be distinct. Our formulation covers the degenerate case $A=A'$ as well, where it reads $I=I_0$; a reader who insists that parallel lines be distinct may simply add the hypothesis $l>0$ throughout, and nothing changes.)

**Definition 3 (Distance to a set; distance between parallel lines).**
For $r\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\emptyset\neq S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$ put $d(r,S):=\inf_{q\in S}|r-q|$. For nonempty sets $S,T$ put $d(S,T):=\inf\{|q-q'| : q\in S,\ q'\in T\}$. The *distance between two parallel lines* $A,A'$ is $l:=d(A,A')$. (Lemma 2 below shows that this infimum is attained and equals the common length of the perpendicular segments between the two lines, which is the usual geometric meaning of the phrase.)

**Definition 4 (Moment of inertia).**
The moment of inertia of $B$ about an axis $L$ is
$$I(L) \;:=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} d(r,L)^2 \, dm \;\in\;[0,+\infty].$$
The integrand $r\mapsto d(r,L)^2$ is continuous, hence Borel measurable (indeed $r\mapsto d(r,L)$ is $1$-Lipschitz, being an infimum of the $1$-Lipschitz functions $r \mapsto |r-q|$; an explicit formula is given in Lemma 1). So the integral is well defined as an element of $[0,+\infty]$. We deliberately allow the value $+\infty$ and prove the theorem as an identity in $[0,+\infty]$, so that no *a priori* finiteness assumption on the moments of inertia is required.

**Definition 5 (Centre of mass).**
Assume
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |r| \, dm < \infty, \tag{H2}$$
so that the vector-valued integral $\int r\,dm$ exists (componentwise, as a Lebesgue integral). The *centre of mass* of $B$ is
$$R_{\mathrm{cm}} := \frac{1}{M}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} r \, dm ,$$
which is the unique point $R$ satisfying $\int (r-R)\,dm=0$: indeed, by (H1) and (H2), $\int (r-R)\,dm = \int r\,dm - MR$, and this vanishes iff $R=R_{\mathrm{cm}}$.

Hypotheses (H1) and (H2) are exactly what is needed for the phrase "a body of mass $M$ possessing a centre of mass" to make sense; they hold automatically for a bounded body of positive finite mass. Remark 3 below shows that (H2) can be weakened.

---

## 2. Four lemmas

Throughout this section fix a unit vector $n$ and let
$$P v := v - (v\cdot n)\,n \qquad (v\in\mathbb{R}^3)$$
be the orthogonal projection onto the plane $n^{\perp}=\{v: v\cdot n=0\}$.

**Lemma 0 (Properties of $P$).** $P$ is linear; $Pv\cdot n=0$ for every $v$; $Pv=v$ whenever $v\cdot n = 0$; and for every $v$,
$$v=Pv+(v\cdot n)n, \quad \text{with } Pv\perp n, \qquad\text{whence}\qquad |v|^2=|Pv|^2+(v\cdot n)^2 .$$

*Proof.* Linearity holds because $v\mapsto (v\cdot n)n$ is linear. Since $|n|=1$, $Pv\cdot n=v\cdot n-(v\cdot n)(n\cdot n)=0$. If $v\cdot n=0$ then $Pv=v$ directly from the definition. The decomposition $v=Pv+(v\cdot n)n$ is immediate from the definition; its two summands are orthogonal (the first is $\perp n$, the second is a scalar multiple of $n$), so the Pythagorean theorem gives $|v|^2=|Pv|^2+|(v\cdot n)n|^2=|Pv|^2+(v\cdot n)^2$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 1 (Distance from a point to a line).** For $L=L(p,n)$ and any $r\in\mathbb{R}^3$,
$$d(r,L)=\bigl|P(r-p)\bigr| ,$$
and the infimum defining $d(r,L)$ is attained, at the unique point $q^*=p+((r-p)\cdot n)\,n$ of $L$.

*Proof.* Write $w:=r-p$. For $t\in\mathbb{R}$, using the decomposition of Lemma 0 applied to $w$,
$$|r-(p+tn)|^2=|w-tn|^2=\bigl|Pw+\bigl((w\cdot n)-t\bigr)n\bigr|^2=|Pw|^2+\bigl((w\cdot n)-t\bigr)^2,$$
the last equality by Pythagoras, since $Pw\perp n$ and $|n|=1$. As a function of $t$ this is $\ge |Pw|^2$, with equality iff $t=w\cdot n$. Since $q\mapsto t$ is a bijection $L\to\mathbb{R}$, taking the infimum over $q\in L$ gives $d(r,L)^2=|Pw|^2$, attained exactly at $q^*=p+(w\cdot n)n$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2 (Distance between parallel lines).** Let $A=L(p,n)$ and $A'=L(p',n)$ be parallel, and set $a:=P(p'-p)$. Then $a\perp n$,
$$A'=\{\,p+a+tn \;:\; t\in\mathbb{R}\,\}=L(p+a,\,n),$$
and $d(A,A')=|a|$, the infimum being attained (e.g. by the pair $p\in A$, $p+a\in A'$).

*Proof.* Put $c:=p'-p$ and $a:=Pc$; by Lemma 0, $c=a+(c\cdot n)n$ and $a\perp n$. Hence
$$A'=\{p+c+tn : t\in\mathbb{R}\}=\bigl\{p+a+\bigl((c\cdot n)+t\bigr)n : t\in\mathbb{R}\bigr\}=\{p+a+sn : s\in\mathbb{R}\},$$
the last step because $t\mapsto s:=(c\cdot n)+t$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$ onto itself. This proves the description of $A'$.

For the distance, a generic pair of points is $q=p+tn\in A$, $q'=p+a+sn\in A'$, and since $a\perp n$, Pythagoras gives
$$|q'-q|^2=|a+(s-t)n|^2=|a|^2+(s-t)^2\ \ge\ |a|^2 ,$$
with equality iff $s=t$. Hence $d(A,A')=|a|$ and the infimum is attained. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3 (Integrability).** Assume (H1) and let $L$ be an axis with $I(L)<\infty$. Then $r\mapsto d(r,L)$ is $\mu$-integrable, with $\int d(r,L)\,dm\le \sqrt{M\,I(L)}$.

*Proof.* Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $L^2(\mu)$ to the nonnegative measurable function $g(r):=d(r,L)$ and the constant function $1$ (both in $L^2(\mu)$, by hypothesis and by (H1) respectively):
$$\int g\,dm \le \Bigl(\int g^2\,dm\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\int 1\,dm\Bigr)^{1/2}=\sqrt{I(L)\,M}<\infty. \qquad \blacksquare$$

---

## 3. The theorem

**Theorem (Huygens–Steiner).** Let $B$ be a body satisfying (H1) and (H2), of mass $M$ and centre of mass $R_{\mathrm{cm}}$. Let $A$ be an axis with $R_{\mathrm{cm}}\in A$, let $A'$ be an axis parallel to $A$, and let $l:=d(A,A')$. Put $I_0:=I(A)$ and $I:=I(A')$. Then
$$\boxed{\,I=I_0+M\,l^2\,}$$
as an identity in $[0,+\infty]$. In particular $I_0<\infty$ if and only if $I<\infty$.

*Proof.* **Set-up.** Let $n$ be a unit direction vector of $A$ and let $P$ be as in Section 2. Since $R_{\mathrm{cm}}\in A$ we may take $R_{\mathrm{cm}}$ as base point:
$$A=L(R_{\mathrm{cm}},n).$$
Since $A'$ is parallel to $A$, we may write $A'=L(p',n)$, and Lemma 2 (applied with $p=R_{\mathrm{cm}}$) yields
$$A'=L(R_{\mathrm{cm}}+a,\;n),\qquad a:=P(p'-R_{\mathrm{cm}})\perp n,\qquad |a|=d(A,A')=l. \tag{3.1}$$

Introduce the position vector relative to the centre of mass and its transverse part:
$$w(r):=r-R_{\mathrm{cm}},\qquad u(r):=P\,w(r)\in n^{\perp} .$$
By Definition 5,
$$\int w(r)\,dm=\int (r-R_{\mathrm{cm}})\,dm=0. \tag{3.2}$$

**The two moments of inertia.** By Lemma 1 applied to $A=L(R_{\mathrm{cm}},n)$ and to $A'=L(R_{\mathrm{cm}}+a,n)$, and using linearity of $P$ together with $Pa=a$ (Lemma 0, since $a\perp n$),
$$d(r,A)=|P(r-R_{\mathrm{cm}})|=|u|,\qquad d(r,A')=\bigl|P\bigl(r-R_{\mathrm{cm}}-a\bigr)\bigr|=|Pw-Pa|=|u-a| .$$
Hence
$$I_0=\int |u|^2\,dm,\qquad I=\int |u-a|^2\,dm. \tag{3.3}$$
Expanding the second integrand pointwise (a purely algebraic identity, using $|a|=l$):
$$|u-a|^2=|u|^2-2\,u\cdot a+|a|^2=|u|^2-2\,u\cdot a+l^2. \tag{3.4}$$
All functions occurring here are Borel measurable, being continuous functions of $r$.

**Case 1: $I_0=+\infty$.** We show $I=+\infty$, so that both sides of the asserted identity equal $+\infty$ (note $Ml^2<\infty$ by (H1)). For all real $x$ and $l$,
$$(x-l)^2-\Bigl(\tfrac12 x^2-l^2\Bigr)=\tfrac12x^2-2lx+2l^2=\tfrac12\bigl(x-2l\bigr)^2\ \ge\ 0,\qquad\text{so}\qquad (x-l)^2\ \ge\ \tfrac12x^2-l^2 .$$
By the reverse triangle inequality, $|u-a|\ \ge\ \bigl||u|-|a|\bigr|=\bigl||u|-l\bigr|$; squaring (both sides being nonnegative) and applying the displayed inequality with $x=|u(r)|$ gives, pointwise in $r$,
$$|u-a|^2\ \ge\ \bigl(|u|-l\bigr)^2\ \ge\ \tfrac12|u|^2-l^2,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad |u-a|^2+l^2\ \ge\ \tfrac12|u|^2 .$$
All three functions $|u-a|^2$, $l^2$, $\tfrac12|u|^2$ are nonnegative and measurable, so monotonicity and additivity of the integral for nonnegative measurable functions (no $\infty-\infty$ arises) give
$$I+Ml^2=\int\bigl(|u-a|^2+l^2\bigr)\,dm\ \ge\ \tfrac12\int|u|^2\,dm=\tfrac12 I_0=+\infty .$$
Since $Ml^2<\infty$, this forces $I=+\infty$, and therefore $I=+\infty=I_0+Ml^2$, as claimed.

**Case 2: $I_0<\infty$.** By Lemma 3 applied to $L=A$, the function $|u|=d(\cdot,A)$ is $\mu$-integrable. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $\mathbb{R}^3$, $|u\cdot a|\le |u|\,|a|=l\,|u|$, so $u\cdot a$ is $\mu$-integrable too; and the constant $l^2$ is $\mu$-integrable by (H1). Since $|u|^2$ is integrable by assumption, every term on the right-hand side of (3.4) is $\mu$-integrable, hence so is the left-hand side, and we may integrate (3.4) term by term (linearity of the Lebesgue integral on integrable functions):
$$I=\int|u|^2\,dm-2\int u\cdot a\,dm+\int l^2\,dm=I_0-2\int (u\cdot a)\,dm+M l^2 . \tag{3.5}$$

**The cross term vanishes.** This is the only place where the hypothesis $R_{\mathrm{cm}}\in A$ is used. Choose an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,n)$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $e_1,e_2\in n^{\perp}$, and write $a=\alpha_1e_1+\alpha_2e_2$ (possible since $a\perp n$). Writing $w(r)=x_1(r)e_1+x_2(r)e_2+x_3(r)n$, we have $u=Pw=x_1e_1+x_2e_2$ and therefore
$$u\cdot a=\alpha_1x_1+\alpha_2x_2 .$$
Each $x_i=w\cdot e_i$ is $\mu$-integrable, since $|x_i|\le|w|\le |r|+|R_{\mathrm{cm}}|$, which is $\mu$-integrable by (H1) and (H2). So by linearity of the integral and by (3.2),
$$\int (u\cdot a)\,dm=\alpha_1\int x_1\,dm+\alpha_2\int x_2\,dm=\alpha_1\Bigl(\int w\,dm\Bigr)\!\cdot e_1+\alpha_2\Bigl(\int w\,dm\Bigr)\!\cdot e_2=0 .$$
Substituting into (3.5) gives $I=I_0+Ml^2$.

In both cases $I=I_0+Ml^2$. Finally, since $Ml^2$ is a finite nonnegative real number, this identity in $[0,+\infty]$ forces $I<\infty\iff I_0<\infty$. $\blacksquare$

---

## 4. Remarks

**Remark 1 (The classical special cases).** For a finite system of point masses $m_i$ at $r_i$ the theorem reads
$$\sum_{i} m_i\,d(r_i,A')^2=\sum_{i} m_i\,d(r_i,A)^2+\Bigl(\sum_i m_i\Bigr)l^2 ,$$
and for a solid $V$ of density $\rho$,
$$\int_V \rho\, d(r,A')^2\,dV=\int_V \rho\,d(r,A)^2\,dV+Ml^2 .$$
Both are instances of the Theorem, via Examples (i) and (ii) of Definition 1.

**Remark 2 (The hypothesis $R_{\mathrm{cm}}\in A$ is essential).** Let $B$ consist of two equal point masses $m$ at $(\pm d,0,0)$ with $d>0$, so that $M=2m$ and $R_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$. Let $A_1,A_2$ be the lines through $(d,0,0)$ and $(-d,0,0)$ with direction $n=e_3$; they are parallel at distance $l=2d$, and by symmetry
$$I(A_1)=I(A_2)=m\cdot 0^2+m\cdot(2d)^2=4md^2 .$$
The formula "$I(A_2)=I(A_1)+Ml^2$" would read $4md^2=4md^2+8md^2$, which is false. So the theorem genuinely needs one of the two axes to pass through the centre of mass. In general, if $A_1,A_2$ are parallel axes at distances $l_1,l_2$ from the axis $A$ through the centre of mass parallel to them, two applications of the Theorem give the correct relation
$$I(A_2)-I(A_1)=M\bigl(l_2^2-l_1^2\bigr)$$
(valid whenever $I(A)<\infty$, so that the subtraction makes sense), which reduces to the stated formula precisely when $l_1=0$, i.e. when $A_1=A$ passes through the centre of mass.

**Remark 3 (Weakening (H2)).** Hypothesis (H2) was used only to define $R_{\mathrm{cm}}$ and to integrate $x_1,x_2$ term by term. In fact, for an axis $A=L(p,n)$ with $I(A)<\infty$, Lemma 3 shows that $|P(r-p)|=d(r,A)$ is $\mu$-integrable, so the vector $\int P(r-p)\,dm$ is defined without any appeal to (H2). The proof of Case 2 then yields, verbatim, the following sharper statement: *if (H1) holds, $A=L(p,n)$ satisfies the transverse centring condition*
$$\int P(r-p)\,dm=0$$
*(which holds in particular when $R_{\mathrm{cm}}\in A$, by (3.2)), and $A'$ is parallel to $A$ at distance $l$, then $I(A')=I(A)+Ml^2$.* Geometrically the condition says that $A$ passes through the centroid of the orthogonal projection of the mass distribution onto the plane $n^\perp$. When $I(A)=+\infty$, Case 1 needs no centring hypothesis at all: $I(A')=+\infty$ for every axis $A'$ parallel to $A$.

**Remark 4 (Minimality).** Since $M l^2\ge0$, with equality iff $l=0$ (as $M>0$), the Theorem shows that among all axes with a given direction, the one through the centre of mass minimises the moment of inertia; and if $I_0<\infty$ the minimum is strict, i.e. $I>I_0$ for every parallel axis $A'\ne A$.
